fatal_errors: The proposed SPS intervention does not reconstruct the target liquid-metal dealloying of a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h.
It treats the starting material as an existing W–Cu composite rather than a single-BCC WTaVTi dendrite–interdendrite alloy whose Ti/V-rich channels are selectively replaced by Cu.
It omits the central selective Ti–Cu exchange mechanism, retention of W/Ta/V-rich RHEA ligaments, and formation of the approximately 300 nm W-rich passivating interlayer.

It claims improved irradiation-stable thermal conductivity without supporting evidence; the target irradiation result concerns He-induced swelling of precursor dendrites as a proxy, not conductivity of irradiated finished joints.
No prior evidence is cited, and the processing and service conditions are too unspecified to support the claimed outcome.
explanation: The response recognizes the broad engineering objectives of reducing interfacial defects and improving heat transfer in W/Cu-related structures, and its controlled SPS-versus-conventional-sintering comparison is reasonably falsifiable. However, it misses nearly every target-specific element: the WTaVTi precursor, directional chemical segregation, molten-Cu dealloying, exact processing window, bicontinuous RHEA–Cu architecture, W-rich interlayer, and measured temperature-dependent thermal behavior. Its generic pressure-assisted densification mechanism is scientifically possible as an alternative processing idea, but it is not supported by cited evidence and does not address the immiscibility and selective-replacement chemistry central to the target. Irradiation boundaries are especially weak because irradiation type, energy, fluence, and the distinction between proxy ligament testing and full-composite testing are absent.
